missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe how, when substances change state (melt, freeze, boil, evaporate, condense or sublimate), mass is conserved.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never says that mass is conserved during a change of state.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Changes of state are physical changes which differ from chemical changes because the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never says that changes of state are physical changes. It does not explain how they differ from chemical changes, or that the material gets its original properties back when the change is reversed.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: When a change of state occurs, the energy supplied changes the energy stored (internal energy) but not the temperature.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson explains this using particle 'potential energy' only. It never links latent heat to the energy stored, or to internal energy as the specification requires.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: AT 5 ... Perform an experiment to measure the latent heat of fusion of water.
missing_spec_content.why: There is no description of an experiment to measure the specific latent heat of fusion of water.

above_gcse.text: Freeze-drying food: food is frozen. Then it is put somewhere with low pressure, so the ice sublimates straight to vapour.
above_gcse.why: Freeze-drying and the effect of low pressure on sublimation are not in the specification. This could confuse the student.

above_gcse.text: Refrigerators: a working fluid (refrigerant) is pumped around a circuit. Inside the fridge it evaporates.
above_gcse.why: The refrigeration cycle is not in these specification sections. The tutor_note also calls it "a classic 6-mark question", which these sections do not support.

above_gcse.text: Heat ice from -10°C to 0°C: Q = mcΔT = 1 × 2100 × 10 = 21,000 J
above_gcse.why: This four-step combined calculation brings in a specific heat capacity for ice. Neither the calculation nor that value is required by these specification sections.

factual_errors.text: Steam burns = DOUBLE the energy. You get L_v as it condenses, THEN Q = mcΔT as it cools.
factual_errors.correction: It is not double. For 1 kg cooling from 100°C to about 37°C, cooling gives about 265 kJ, while condensing gives about 2260 kJ. That makes steam roughly 9 to 10 times the energy of the same mass of boiling water.

factual_errors.text: Outside the fridge it condenses. It releases that latent heat to the surroundings. This is why the back of a fridge is warm.
factual_errors.correction: The condenser also gives out the energy supplied by the compressor. The warmth at the back is not only the latent heat taken in from the fridge contents.
